record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study extracts a harmful-minus-benign difference-in-means refusal direction and tests directional weight orthogonalization on two chat models, reporting post-abliteration refusal scores.
record.gate_note: The hyperparameter-selection results are not recorded as findings. Utility benchmarks are for AMRA and comparator defenses, not for models after ablation, so they do not test capability preservation under the claimed removal. HarmBench ASR and LlamaGuard unsafe rates are safety measures, not refusal scores.
record.test_reason: The paper is a defense study, but it also reports the undefended baseline: difference-in-means (harmful minus harmless) direction extraction and Arditi-style weight orthogonalization on Llama-3-8B and Gemma-2-9B, with clean and post-abliteration refusal scores (Table 1). Those two baseline rows bear on V1 (ablation removes refusal) and V2 (weight edit removes refusal in released models). All other rows compare the authors' defense with other defenses.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that AMRA improves post-abliteration refusal on both models: by 2.16 points on Llama-3-8B with under 0.5 pp MMLU loss, and by 14.70 points on Gemma-2-9B at a larger utility cost, with Gemma's post-abliteration score still negative. They say targeting extraction of the refusal direction is a viable defense. 'Harder extraction' is their interpretation; they do not measure it directly.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful-versus-benign difference-in-means extraction and directional weight orthogonalization, but selects causally relevant layers and evaluates a defense against ablation rather than testing the full original intervention set.
record.method_sensitivity: Architecture and defense condition change the post-abliteration score; AMRA improves that score more on Gemma-2-9B than on Llama-3-8B.

fits_no_version.finding: A post-hoc rank-k weight edit (AMRA) that aliases refusal activations at writer matrices raises post-abliteration refusal scores. On Llama they go from 5.69 to 7.85; on Gemma from -16.01 to -1.31. Other defenses (Circuit Breakers, CAST) barely change Gemma's post-abliteration score.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Obscuring the extractability of the difference-in-means direction, without training, makes models more robust to abliteration.

record.problems: Only two model architectures and a single directional-ablation attack are tested. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The utility benchmarks measure AMRA and comparator models before ablation, not general capability after ablation.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal. Capability preservation after ablation: utility is measured only for defended models, not ablated ones. Per-layer ablation ASR is used for AMRA layer selection but not reported.
Released models other than Llama-3-8B and Gemma-2-9B. Other abliteration tools. Utility of the abliterated models.

record.verdict_notes: Only r1 and r7 (undefended models) bear on the claim; the rest is defense comparison. The refusal score is not defined in the text and is presumably Arditi's log-odds metric. No uncertainty is reported. The attack's layer and direction-selection procedure is not described, so the weak Llama result may reflect implementation choices rather than a property of the model. The Table 1 caption is garbled about when extraction was re-run after defenses.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test adding the direction to induce refusals, ablation at every layer and position, or whether general abilities remain intact after ablation.
The study tests directional weight orthogonalization on Llama-3-8B and Gemma-2-9B, but not other released models or ablation methods.
